 1                        MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

 2   I.      INTRODUCTION

 3           It is widely recognized that employees in the technology industry frequently move

 4   between companies—including direct competitors—as part of ordinary career progression. 1

 5   This mobility is a hallmark of Silicon Valley and is protected by California’s long-standing

 6   policy favoring employee freedom and open competition. See Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP,

 7   44 Cal. 4th 937, 946 (2008). Such transitions are common practice, not cause for suspicion.

 8           Yet Plaintiff Apple Inc. (“Apple”) attempts to portray its former employee, Defendant

 9   Chen Shi (“Dr. Shi”), as a wrongdoer for doing exactly what thousands of engineers in this

10   District do every year—pursuing a new opportunity with another technology company. Apple’s

11   Complaint cobbles together a hodgepodge of ordinary workplace events—text messages, internal

12   meetings, and routine file access—into a speculative narrative of misconduct, without alleging a

13   single concrete fact showing that Dr. Shi used or disclosed any confidential information after

14   leaving Apple.

15           Apple asserts a single claim against Dr. Shi for breach of his employee confidentiality

16   agreement (the “IPA”), but that claim fails as a matter of law. As explained below, the IPA is

17   void under California Business and Professions Code § 16600 because it sweeps far beyond the

18   protection of trade secrets and operates as an unlawful restraint on Dr. Shi’s right to work. Even

19   if it were enforceable, Apple pleads no facts showing a breach, as the Complaint contains no

20   factual allegation that Dr. Shi transferred, used, or disclosed any confidential information outside

21   of Apple. Finally, Apple fails to allege any resulting harm, offering only boilerplate assertions of

22   “irreparable injury.”

23           The issue to be decided is whether Apple’s conclusory allegations—that Dr. Shi

24   supposedly “transferred” or “used” confidential information, without identifying any specific

25   information, disclosure, or injury—are sufficient to state a plausible claim for breach of contract

26
     1 Sumit Upadhyay, The Job Hopping Phenomenon: A Case Study on Employees Changing Jobs Every 2-3 Years,
27
     LinkedIn (June 8, 2024), https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/job-hopping-phenomenon-case-study-employees-
28   changing-jobs-upadhyay‐b4ptf/
     .

                                                        -1-
     DEFENDANT CHEN SHI’S MOTION TO DISMISS                                     CASE NO. 5:25-CV-07105-EKL
      Case 5:25-cv-07105-EKL          Document 94       Filed 10/20/25      Page 7 of 16



 1   under Rule 12(b)(6). They are not. Apple’s Complaint rests on speculation and inference rather

 2   than well-pleaded facts, and should therefore be dismissed in its entirety.

 3   II.     FACTUAL BACKGROUND

 4           After obtaining his Ph.D. from Columbia University in electrical engineering focused on

 5   biomechanical devices, Dr. Shi began work at Apple in or around January 2020 as a Sensor

 6   System Architect.

 7           According to the Complaint, Dr. Shi executed the IPA before starting his first day at

 8   Apple. Dkt. No. 1 (“Compl.”) ¶ 4. The IPA legally obligates Apple employees to protect and not

 9   disclose Apple’s confidential information to unauthorized third parties and is clear that this

10   obligation continues after an employee leaves Apple. Compl. ¶ 54. Specifically, the IPA calls

11   such confidential information “Proprietary Information,” and defines it, in relevant part, as:

12           All information not generally known outside Apple and/or kept confidential by Apple,
             including for example but not limited to (a) trade secrets, R&D records, reports, samples,
13           manuals, plans, specifications, inventions, ideas, designs, prototypes, software, source
             code, or any other materials or information relating to past, existing, and future products
14           and services whether or not developed, marketed, used, or rejected by Apple or persons
             or companies dealing with Apple [. . ..]
15
     Compl. Ex. 2 at 3.
16

17           While Dr. Shi was generally content with his position and role at Apple, he desired to
18   broaden his experience to other areas of health sensing. To learn more about such areas, he
19   regularly met 1-on-1 with other Apple employees. In its Complaint, however, Apple claims that
20   such meetings “were in furtherance of Defendants’ illegal and improper scheme” because Dr. Shi
21   had “no legitimate business purpose for arranging these meetings, which covered projects that
22   Dr. Shi was not involved with at Apple, including about future technologies beyond the scope of
23   Dr. Shi’s role.” Id. ¶ 73.
24           Believing his potential at Apple to be somewhat limited, in early 2025 Dr. Shi began to
25   explore career opportunities with companies in similar fields. He learned that Dr. Zijing Zeng, an
26   employee of Defendant Guangdong OPPO Mobile Telecommunications Corp., Ltd. (“OPPO”)
27   had moved from Apple to lead the OPPO Health team, and connected with him in April 2025
28   initially to seek his advice on career advancement.

                                                     -2-
     DEFENDANT CHEN SHI’S MOTION TO DISMISS                                CASE NO. 5:25-CV-07105-EKL
      Case 5:25-cv-07105-EKL          Document 94        Filed 10/20/25      Page 8 of 16



 1           As Apple itself admits, Dr. Shi used his Apple-issued work devices to communicate with

 2   Dr. Zeng. Id. ¶ 65. In or around May 2025, the two discussed an open position at OPPO, and Dr.

 3   Shi decided to join the company. Id. ¶ 70.

 4           In the weeks leading up to Dr. Shi’s resignation from Apple, he allegedly transferred

 5   approximately 63 files from Apple’s shared file site at Box (the “Box files”) into a folder called

 6   “Apple Related” on his Apple-issued MacBook. Id. ¶ 78. Of the 63 Box files, however, Apple

 7   only identifies 10 files as allegedly trade secret and confidential documents. Id. ¶ 80.

 8           Apple then alleges that Dr. Shi copied the “Apple Related” folder from the Apple-issued

 9   MacBook to his USB hard drive, but does not, and in fact cannot allege that Dr. Shi copied the

10   Box files to his USB hard drive. Id. ¶ 81 (emphasis added).

11           Rather, Apple alleges that the folder structures on the USB hard drive are the same as the

12   folder structures on Dr. Shi’s Apple-issued MacBook, which “evidences his wholesale copying

13   of that folder.” Id.

14            Apple admits that “departing employees must return Apple devices, including laptops

15   and mobile devices, as well as their badges and other Apple-owned equipment.” Id. ¶ 81. Since

16   Apple was able to inspect Dr. Shi’s Apple-issued work devices (and in fact has extensively

17   referred in the Complaint to communications it retrieved from such devices), it follows that Dr.

18   Shi complied with Apple policy and returned his Apple-issued work devices, including the

19   Apple-issued MacBook, before June 27, 2025, his last day at the company. See id. ¶ 65.

20           Notably, Apple does not make any factual allegations that Dr. Shi has either used or

21   disclosed the Box files, or any other proprietary information since leaving Apple. Apple only

22   alleges in a conclusory fashion that Dr. Shi transferred, published, disclosed, or reported Apple’s

23   proprietary information not generally known outside of Apple and used such information outside

24   the course of performing his duties for Apple and other than for the sole benefit of Apple.

25   Compl. ¶ 112.

26           Apple further alleges that as a proximate result of Dr. Shi’s actions, Apple was damaged

27   and has suffered “irreparable harm.” Id. ¶¶ 112-114. However, Apple fails to provide any details

28   about the alleged injury.


                                                     -3-
     DEFENDANT CHEN SHI’S MOTION TO DISMISS                                CASE NO. 5:25-CV-07105-EKL
      Case 5:25-cv-07105-EKL          Document 94         Filed 10/20/25      Page 9 of 16



 1   III.   LEGAL STANDARD

 2          To survive a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim under Rule 12(b)(6), “a

 3   complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is

 4   plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v.

 5   Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). A claim has facial plausibility only “when the plaintiff

 6   pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is

 7   liable for the misconduct alleged.” Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678 (citing Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556).

 8          However, the Court is not required to accept as true “allegations that are merely

 9   conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.” In re Gilead Scis. Sec.

10   Litig., 536 F.3d 1049, 1055 (9th Cir. 2008). A plaintiff’s “[f]actual allegations must be enough to

11   raise a right to relief above the speculative level.” Twombly, 550 U.S. at 545. “A pleading that

12   offers ‘labels and conclusions’ or ‘a formulaic recitation of the elements of a cause of action will

13   not do.’ Nor does a complaint suffice if it tenders ‘naked assertion[s]’ devoid of ‘further factual

14   enhancement.’” Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678 (internal citation omitted). “While legal conclusions can

15   provide the framework of a complaint, they must be supported by factual allegations.” Id. at 679.

16   In assessing a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), a two-prong approach is used. Id. First, the

17   court discounts conclusory statements, and second, the court determines whether any of the

18   factual allegations, which are assumed as true, plausibly give rise to relief. Iqbal, 556 U.S. at

19   679-80.

20          This Court has held that absent an additional detail explaining the basis of its beliefs, an

21   allegation made only on “information and belief” is merely a surplusage and thus “creates a

22   further inference that plaintiff likely lacks knowledge of underlying facts to support the assertion,

23   and is instead engaging in speculation to an undue degree.” Delphix Corp. v. Actifo, Inc., No.

24   5:13-cv-04613-BLF, 2014 WL 4628490, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 19, 2014).

25   IV.    ARGUMENT

26          A.      Apple’s Breach of Contract Claim Against Dr. Shi Fails to State a Claim

27                  upon Which Relief Can Be Granted

28


                                                      -4-
     DEFENDANT CHEN SHI’S MOTION TO DISMISS                                 CASE NO. 5:25-CV-07105-EKL
      Case 5:25-cv-07105-EKL         Document 94        Filed 10/20/25     Page 10 of 16



 1          Apple alleges that Dr. Shi breached the IPA by not holding Apple’s proprietary

 2   information in confidence and by transferring, publishing, disclosing, or reporting Apple’s

 3   proprietary information not generally known outside of Apple and using such information

 4   outside the course of performing his duties for Apple and other than for the sole benefit of Apple.

 5   Compl. ¶ 112. Dr. Shi further allegedly breached the IPA by “transferring materials and property

 6   belonging to Apple, including by transferring Apple’s trade secret documents to a personal

 7   external storage drive for his and the OPPO Defendants’ ongoing possession and use.” Id. ¶ 113.

 8          A claim for breach of contract requires “(1) the existence of the contract; (2) plaintiff’s

 9   performance or excuse of nonperformance; (3) defendant’s breach; and (4) damages to plaintiff

10   as a result of the breach.” Gutierrez v. State Farm Ins. Co., No. 12-5846 PSG, 2013 WL

11   2403651, at *5 (N.D. Cal. May 31, 2013) (citation omitted). Apple has failed to state a claim for

12   breach of contract for three reasons. First, Apple does not plead a valid contract because the IPA

13   is void as an unlawful restraint of trade under California Business and Professions Code Section

14   16600. Second, Apple fails to plead facts that plausibly suggest Dr. Shi breached the IPA. Third,

15   Apple has failed to assert an injury resulting from Dr. Shi’s alleged breach.

16                  1.      The IPA Is Void as an Unlawful Restraint of Trade.

17          Apple has not pleaded, and cannot plead, the existence of a valid contract. California

18   Business and Professions Code Section 16600 states that “every contract by which anyone is

19   restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent

20   void.” California courts “have consistently affirmed that section 16600 evinces a settled

21   legislative policy in favor of open competition and employee mobility.” Edwards v. Arthur

22   Andersen LLP, 44 Cal. 4th 937, 946 (2008) (citing D’Sa v. Playhut, Inc., 85 Cal. App. 4th 927,

23   933 (2000)). Following Edwards, cases are clear that contracts that are not tailored to trade secret

24   protection are unenforceable. See Dowell v. Biosense Webster, Inc., 179 Cal. App. 4th 564, 576

25   (2009); see also Richmond Techs., Inc. v. Aumtech Bus. Solutions, No. 11-CV-2460-LHK, 2011

26   WL 2607158, at *18 (N.D. Cal. July 1, 2011) (noting that broad employment agreements not

27   targeted at protecting employer trade secrets “are likely to be found unenforceable under

28   California law.”)

 1          Dowell is particularly instructive. There, the plaintiff sued its former employees for

 2   breach of a broadly worded “Employee Secrecy, Non-Competition and Non-Solicitation

 3   Agreement.” 179 Cal. App. 4th at 567-68. That agreement purported to restrict the former

 4   employees’ use of “CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION,” a term defined to include “information

 5   disclosed to [the employee] or known by [her] as a result of [her] employment by the

 6   COMPANY… about products, processes, technologies, machines, customers, clients,

 7   employees, services and strategies of the COMPANY.” Id. at 568. The Court held that this

 8   agreement was void and unenforceable as an unlawful restraint of trade under Section 16600. Id.

 9   at 574–75. Specifically, the Dowell court held that whether or not a “trade secret exception”

10   exists to Section 16600, the agreement at issue was “not narrowly tailored or carefully limited to

11   the protection of trade secrets, but [] so broadly worded as to restrain competition.” Id. at 577–

12   78.

13          Here, as in Dowell, the IPA is void under Section 16600. Apple alleges that Dr. Shi

14   breached the IPA, which purports to restrict use of Apple’s “Proprietary Information,” a broad

15   umbrella term defined to include more than just trade secrets. Indeed, just like in Dowell, the IPA

16   defined “Proprietary Information” to include “reports,” “manuals,” “plans,” and “specifications,”

17   as well as even broader concepts      such as “designs” and “ideas.” See, e.g., Compl. Ex. 2 at 3.

18   “Proprietary Information” in the IPA is as broad as, if not broader than, the same term used in the

19   unenforceable employee agreement in Dowell. 179 Cal. App. 4th at 578. Indeed, Apple attempts

20   to use this unenforceable provision to restrict Dr. Shi’s pursuit of a career in the health sensing

21   industry—an overbroad restraint on Dr. Shi’s livelihood.

22          Further, as in Dowell, the Court does not need to determine whether a “trade secret

23   exception” to Section 16600 exists to find the IPA void. Apple’s Complaint makes clear that the

24   IPA is not narrowly tailored to protect Apple’s trade secrets. Indeed, the IPA states that it

25   protects not only “trade secrets,” but also information in categories other than trade secrets, such

26   as “personnel information.” Compl. Ex. 2 at 3.

27                  2.      Apple Does Not Adequately Plead a Breach of the IPA

 1          A complaint is deficient “if it tenders ‘naked assertion[s]’ devoid of “further factual

 2   enhancement.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (citing Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly,

 3   550 U.S. 544, 557 (2007)). Yet conclusory allegations and naked assertions are all that Apple

 4   includes in its contract claim.

 5          SriCom, Inc. v. EbisLogi, Inc. is analogous and informative on a plaintiff’s burden to

 6   plead breach. No. 12-cv-904-LHK, 2012 WL 4051222 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 13, 2012). There, the

 7   plaintiff alleged breach of a confidentiality clause in a contract between the parties. 2012 WL

 8   4051222 at *5–6. The complaint alleged that defendants “revealed” vague categories of

 9   information—“customer information, employee information, and pricing information”—but

10   failed to “allege any facts concerning what specific information was revealed, when, how, or to

11   whom it was revealed, or whether or how [the defendants] used this information.” Id. at *6

12   (emphasis added). This Court dismissed the breach of contract claim based on the confidentiality

13   clause because the allegations amounted to a “conclusory assertion that there [had] been a

14   breach, with no factual support.” Id; see also Sensible Foods, LLC v. World Gourmet, Inc., No.

15   11-2819 SC, 2011 WL 5244716, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 3, 2011) (finding “the Complaint states

16   ‘Defendants failed to perform … under the confidentiality agreements [sic], including, but not

17   limited to disclosing all or a portion of Plaintiff’s Confidential Information’ … Such

18   ‘[t]hreadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action’ are insufficient to state a claim under

19   Iqbal”).

20                          a.         Apple Does Not Allege Transfer of Proprietary Information

21          As an initial matter, Apple does not identify the confidential information at issue with

22   specificity. This alone dooms Apple’s breach of contract claim. Artec Grp., Inc. v. Klimov, No.

23   15-CV-03449-EMC, 2016 WL 8223346, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 22, 2016) (dismissing claim for

24   breach of a non-disclosure agreement for failing to “identify with specificity what confidential

25   information is at issue.”). Out of the 63 Box files, Apple vaguely claims that 10 files are “trade

26   secret and confidential documents” but never alleges which parts of these documents have trade

27   secrets or confidential information, or that Dr. Shi even knew that the 63 Box files contained

28   trade secrets and confidential information.

 1          More importantly, Apple does not allege that Dr. Shi copied these 10 “trade secret and

 2   confidential” documents – or any other of the 63 Box files – onto his USB hard drive. The only

 3   factual allegations regarding any “transferring, publishing, disclosing, or reporting Apple’s

 4   proprietary information” are that Dr. Shi transferred the Box files to his Apple-issued MacBook,

 5   which was returned to Apple before his departure. Compl. ¶ 78. Apple’s forensic assertion falls

 6   short of establishing that Dr. Shi copied any files from his work device. Apple alleges that

 7   certain folders on a personal USB drive “had the same folder structure” as those on Dr. Shi’s

 8   Apple-issued MacBook—nothing more. Id. ¶ 81. That observation, even if accurate, does not

 9   amount to an allegation that a transfer occurred, let alone that Dr. Shi engaged in “wholesale

10   copying.” Apple’s conclusion of “copying” is therefore only an inference—one unsupported by

11   technical proof and insufficient to state a plausible claim of breach, because nothing in the IPA

12   prohibits employees from downloading files from Apple’s Box site to their Apple-issued

13   devices, and then returning such Apple-issued devices to Apple.

14                         b.     Apple Fails to Allege Dr. Shi’s Use or Disclosure

15          Apple does not plausibly allege that Dr. Shi actually used or disclosed any proprietary

16   information in violation of the IPA. Instead, Apple relies on conclusory assertions that merely

17   restate the elements of a claim. Apple alleges that Dr. Shi transferred, published, disclosed, or

18   reported Apple’s proprietary information and that he used “such information outside the course

19   of performing his duties for Apple and other than for the sole benefit of Apple.” Compl. ¶ 112.

20   But these allegations are wholly unsupported by facts identifying what information was

21   purportedly disclosed, when or how any disclosure occurred, or to whom. Apple does not

22   identify a single Apple document, file, or communication that Dr. Shi allegedly shared, nor does

23   it allege that OPPO or defendant Innopeak Technology, Inc. (“Innopeak”) ever received or used

24   any Apple information.

25          Such threadbare allegations are insufficient to state a claim for breach. In Pellerin v.

26   Honeywell Int’l, Inc., 877 F. Supp. 2d 983, 989 (S.D. Cal. 2012), the court rejected claims

27   predicated on bare allegations that a former employee disclosed confidential information to a

28   competitor, explaining that a plaintiff must allege facts demonstrating that the information was

26   while still employed by Apple—not any use or disclosure of confidential information outside the

 9                  3.     Apple Has Not Alleged Harm from the Alleged Breach of the IPA

10           Apple has not alleged facts supporting any injury resulting from Dr. Shi’s claimed breach

11   of the IPA. In its complaint, Apple states in conclusory terms that it “has been damaged” and

12   “has suffered and will continue to suffer irreparable harm” as a result of Dr. Shi’s breach.

13   Compl. ¶¶ 114-115. Such conclusory statements of law are not sufficient—to adequately plead a

14   breach of contract claim, Apple must allege specific facts showing that it has actually suffered

15   harm.

16           As courts in this District have found, it is not sufficient to show that an employee

17   “retained information defined in [their] contract as confidential information, in contravention of

18   [a] provision requiring [them] to return confidential material[.]” KLA-Tencor Corp. v. Murphy,

19   717 F. Supp. 2d 895, 907 (N.D. Cal. 2010). Rather, to support a claim for breach of contract, the

20   plaintiff must also “demonstrate[ ] that it was damaged by such conduct.” Id. Facts showing that

21   an employee “used or disclosed” confidential information are required to demonstrate harm. See

22   id. (“plaintiff has not demonstrated that it was damaged by” an employee’s retention of

23   confidential information since “[t]here is not even a suggestion . . . that [the employee] used or

24   disclosed any confidential information”); see also Aguilera v. Pirelli Armstrong Tire Corp., 223

25   F.3d 1010, 1015 (9th Cir. 2000) (“[T]o be actionable, harm must constitute something more than

26   nominal damages, speculative harm, or the threat of future harm-not yet realized ...” (quoting

27   Buttram v. Owens–Corning Fiberglas Corp., 16 Cal.4th 520, 531 n. 4 (1997)). Yet here, Apple

28   has not alleged any facts showing that Dr. Shi has transferred, used, or disclosed Apple’s

 4   V.     CONCLUSION

 5          Apple’s sole claim against Dr. Shi fails as a matter of law. The IPA is void under Section

 6   16600 because it sweeps far beyond protection of trade secrets and operates as an unlawful

 7   restraint on Dr. Shi’s right to work. Even if it were enforceable, Apple does not plead facts

 8   showing a breach: the Complaint identifies no specific proprietary information that Dr. Shi

 9   transferred, used, or disclosed outside Apple, and its reliance on ordinary internal meetings

10   cannot salvage the claim. Finally, Apple alleges no non-speculative injury attributable to Dr.

11   Shi’s purported conduct.

12          For these independent reasons, the Court should dismiss the Complaint with prejudice

13   and grant such further relief as the Court deems just and proper.
